Items.Name: Profile
Items.Doc:
A bundle of compiler options under a name. The toolchain knows `debug` and `release`, and
`lyric build --release` chooses one for the whole build.

The table lives in the toolchain, not here: this asks it, so a build script and `lyrc` can
never disagree about what `release` means.

Members.Name: name
Members.Doc: `debug` or `release`.

Members.Name: optimize
Members.Doc: Whether the IR optimizations run: inlining, scalar replacement, devirtualization.

Members.Name: sourceMap
Members.Doc: Whether the module carries line numbers, for a backtrace that names its line.

Members.Name: debugInfo
Members.Doc: Whether the module carries slot and field names, for a debugger.

Members.Name: denyWarnings
Members.Doc: Whether a warning fails the compile.

Members.Name: selected
Members.Doc: The profile the command line chose (`--release`, `--profile x`); `debug` without a choice.

Members.Name: debug
Members.Doc: The debug profile: no optimizations, every name and line kept.

Members.Name: release
Members.Doc: The release profile: optimized, the line numbers kept, the debug info dropped.

Members.Name: named
Members.Signature: pub static fn named(name: string): Profile
Members.Doc: The toolchain's profile of that name. A name it does not know ends the build.

Items.Name: Kind
Items.Doc: What an artifact is.

Members.Name: Executable
Members.Doc: A program: one `.lyrbc`, compiled whole from its entry file.

Members.Name: Library
Members.Doc: A library: every module under its root checked as a whole, nothing written.

Members.Name: Packed
Members.Doc: A program packed with the stub runtime into one executable.

Items.Name: Artifact
Items.Doc:
One thing a build produces.

A script holds it and configures it after the call that produced it; nothing is read from it
until `build` has returned, so a field set on the next line still applies. Every option
starts from the profile the build was started with, and `use` takes another.

Members.Name: kind
Members.Doc: What it is.

Members.Name: name
Members.Doc: Its name: an identifier, and the stem of the file it lands in.

Members.Name: entry
Members.Doc:
The entry file of a program, or the root directory of a library, relative to the
directory holding `build.lyr`.

Members.Name: profileName
Members.Doc: The profile the options came from. It names the directory under `out/`.

Members.Name: optimize
Members.Doc: Whether the IR optimizations run.

Members.Name: sourceMap
Members.Doc: Whether the module carries line numbers.

Members.Name: debugInfo
Members.Doc: Whether the module carries slot and field names.

Members.Name: denyWarnings
Members.Doc: Whether a warning fails this artifact.

Members.Name: output
Members.Doc:
Where it lands. `null` means `out/<profile>/<name>.lyrbc`, or `out/<profile>/<name>` for a
packed program, where the toolchain adds the platform's executable suffix to an output
without one.

Members.Name: use
Members.Signature: pub mut fn use(profile: Profile): void
Members.Doc:
Takes the options of `profile`, its name included: a tool shipped beside a game that is
still being debugged is `tool.use(Profile.release())`.

Members.Name: outputPath
Members.Doc:
The path it is written to: `output` when set, the derivation above otherwise. Empty for a
library, which writes nothing.

Items.Name: executable
Items.Signature: pub fn executable(name: string, entry: string): Artifact
Items.Doc:
Declares a program: `name` is an identifier, `entry` its main file relative to the project.
It starts with the profile the build was started with.

Items.Name: library
Items.Signature: pub fn library(name: string, root: string): Artifact
Items.Doc: Declares a library: every module under `root` is checked as a whole, and nothing is written.

Items.Name: packed
Items.Doc:
Declares a packed program from an executable's artifact: the same name, entry and options,
packed with the stub runtime once compiled. It lands as `out/<profile>/<name>`.

Items.Name: option
Items.Signature: pub fn option(name: string, help: string): ?string
Items.Doc:
A value from the command line, `-D name=value`: `null` when it was not given, and `""` when
it was given without a value. `help` is what `lyric build --help` shows beside the name.

Items.Name: flag
Items.Signature: pub fn flag(name: string, help: string): bool
Items.Doc: A switch from the command line, `-D name`. `help` is what `lyric build --help` shows.

Items.Name: addExecutable
Items.Signature: pub fn addExecutable(entry: string, output: string): Artifact
Items.Doc:
The 4.x form: the entry first, and the output named outright. It builds as it always did,
named after the output's stem; the name rule is not applied, because a 4.x script never
chose a name.

Items.Name: finish
Items.Doc:
Hands every declared artifact to the toolchain and compiles them. Called by `lyric build`
once `build` has returned, never by a script. Returns how many failed.

Modules.Doc:
Slicing and searching over `uint8[]` — what a wire protocol does between reads.

The edges mirror `string.substring` exactly: a negative `start` or `count` panics, a
`start` past the end panics, and a `count` past the end clamps to it. `indexOf` answers
`-1` when nothing is found — ready for `slice`, as `string.indexOf` is for `substring`.

Items.Name: slice
Items.Signature: pub fn slice(bytes: uint8[], start: int, count: int): uint8[]
Items.Doc: `count` bytes from `start`, clamped at the end like `string.substring`.

Items.Name: indexOf
Items.Signature: pub fn indexOf(bytes: uint8[], value: uint8): int
Items.Doc: The first position of `value`, or `-1` — ready for `slice`.

Items.Name: indexOfFrom
Items.Signature: pub fn indexOfFrom(bytes: uint8[], value: uint8, start: int): int
Items.Doc:
Searches from a position. `-1` when nothing is found, as in `indexOf`; a negative `start`
searches from the front, one past the end finds nothing.

Items.Name: Indexable
Items.Doc:
What can be read and written with `[i]`.

The same model as `Iterator<T>` for `for-in`: the compiler knows one built-in form — the array —
and binds everything else to an interface from the standard library, so there is no special case
per container type.

`get` and `set` are O(1). That is a requirement, not a description: an implementation with O(n)
access must not satisfy this interface, or an index loop would be quadratic without showing it.
`string` has no index operator for the same reason.

Members.Name: get
Members.Doc: The value at `index`.

Members.Name: set
Members.Signature: mut fn set(index: int, value: T): void
Members.Doc: Replaces the value at `index`.

Items.Name: List
Items.Doc:
A growing list; a `T[]` has a fixed length, this does not.

Growing doubles and shrinking halves at a quarter, so `push` is amortized O(1) and a list
oscillating around a boundary does not copy on every step.

Members.Name: data
Members.Doc: The backing slots; optional so a popped slot can actually release its value.

Members.Name: count
Members.Doc: How many slots are filled.

Members.Name: length
Members.Doc: How many values are in it.

Members.Name: empty
Members.Doc: An empty list.

Members.Name: iter
Members.Doc: A fresh cursor on every call, so two loops over the same list do not disturb each other.

Members.Name: of
Members.Signature: pub static fn of(items: T[]): List<T>
Members.Doc:
A list holding the elements of an array, in order: `List<int>.of([3, 1, 2])`. The
array is copied; the list owns its slots.

Members.Name: pushAll
Members.Signature: pub mut fn pushAll(items: T[]): void
Members.Doc: Appends every element of the array, in order.

Members.Name: pushAllFrom
Members.Signature: pub mut fn pushAllFrom(other: List<T>): void
Members.Doc: Appends every element of another list, in order. The other list is unchanged.

Members.Name: slice
Members.Signature: pub fn slice(from: int, to: int): List<T>
Members.Doc:
The elements from `from` up to but not including `to`, as a NEW list. The bounds must
satisfy `0 <= from <= to <= length()`; anything else is a panic, as an index out of
range is — a slice with crossed bounds is a programming error, not an empty answer.

Members.Name: filter
Members.Signature: pub fn filter(keep: fn(T) -> bool): List<T>
Members.Doc: A new list of the elements `keep` accepts, in order, eagerly.

Members.Name: forEach
Members.Signature: pub fn forEach(f: fn(T) -> void): void
Members.Doc: Calls `f` on every element, in order.

Members.Name: removeWhere
Members.Signature: pub mut fn removeWhere(drop: fn(T) -> bool): int
Members.Doc:
Removes every element `drop` accepts, keeping the order of the rest; answers how many
went. One pass, so removing many is O(n) rather than O(n) per removal.

Members.Name: toReversed
Members.Doc: A reversed COPY; `reverse` is the in-place form.

Members.Name: isEmpty
Members.Doc: Whether nothing is in it.

Members.Name: capacity
Members.Doc:
How many slots are allocated, empty ones included. For tests and for anyone measuring what
the list costs; `length` is the truth for everything else.

Members.Name: push
Members.Signature: pub mut fn push(value: T): void
Members.Doc: Appends at the end; amortized O(1).

Members.Name: pop
Members.Doc:
Removes and returns the last value, or `null` for an empty list — an ordinary state,
unlike an index out of range.

Members.Name: get
Members.Doc:
The value at `index`. Out of range is a panic, as for an array: a programming error
rather than a state.

Members.Name: set
Members.Signature: pub mut fn set(index: int, value: T): void
Members.Doc: Replaces the value at `index`. Out of range is a panic, as in `get`.

Members.Name: clear
Members.Doc:
Empties the list. Every slot is released — nothing inserted stays alive — but the
backing array is KEPT: a buffer emptied once per frame must not reallocate on every
refill.

Members.Name: first
Members.Doc: The first value, or `null` for an empty list.

Members.Name: last
Members.Doc: The last value, or `null` for an empty list.

Members.Name: insert
Members.Signature: pub mut fn insert(index: int, value: T): void
Members.Doc:
Inserts at `index`, shifting everything from there one to the right. `index == length()`
appends. Out of range is a panic, as in `get`.

Members.Name: removeAt
Members.Signature: pub mut fn removeAt(index: int): T
Members.Doc:
Removes and returns the value at `index`, shifting the rest left. Out of range is a
panic, as in `get`.

Members.Name: reverse
Members.Doc: Reverses in place.

Members.Name: swap
Members.Signature: pub mut fn swap(a: int, b: int): void
Members.Doc: Exchanges two positions. Out of range is a panic, as in `get`.

Members.Name: toArray
Members.Doc: A copy as a real array.

Items.Name: ListIterator
Items.Doc: Walks a list; each loop holds its own cursor.

Members.Name: source
Members.Doc: The list being walked.

Members.Name: index
Members.Doc: The next slot to look at.

Members.Name: next
Members.Doc: The next value, or `null` at the end.

Items.Name: collect
Items.Doc:
Collects an iterator into a `List<T>`.

Here rather than in `std.iter`, because the dependency runs this way: `std.collections` imports
`std.iter`, not the reverse. `std.iter.collectArray` is the variant without that dependency,
and it is quadratic because a `T[]` copies on every append. This one doubles and is linear.

Items.Name: Deque
Items.Doc:
A double-ended queue: push and pop are O(1) at BOTH ends.

Deliberately without iteration for now: a run queue is drained, not walked, and `popFront`
in a loop IS its walk. `null` from a pop or peek means "empty" — an ordinary state, like a
`List` pop, and the whole truth, so there is no throwing twin.

Members.Name: data
Members.Doc: The backing ring; optional so a popped slot releases its value.

Members.Name: head
Members.Doc: The index of the front value, meaningful while `count > 0`.

Members.Name: count
Members.Doc: How many slots are filled.

Members.Name: empty
Members.Doc: An empty deque.

Members.Name: length
Members.Doc: How many values are in it.

Members.Name: isEmpty
Members.Doc: Whether nothing is in it.

Members.Name: toArray
Members.Doc: The elements front to back as an array — a look at the queue without draining it.

Members.Name: capacity
Members.Doc:
How many slots are allocated, empty ones included. For tests and for anyone measuring
what the deque costs; `length` is the truth for everything else.

Members.Name: pushBack
Members.Signature: pub mut fn pushBack(value: T): void
Members.Doc: Appends at the back; amortized O(1).

Members.Name: pushFront
Members.Signature: pub mut fn pushFront(value: T): void
Members.Doc: Prepends at the front; amortized O(1) — the ring is the reason no slot moves.

Members.Name: popFront
Members.Doc: Removes and returns the front value, or `null` when empty.

Members.Name: popBack
Members.Doc: Removes and returns the back value, or `null` when empty.

Members.Name: peekFront
Members.Doc: The front value without removing it, or `null` when empty.

Members.Name: peekBack
Members.Doc: The back value without removing it, or `null` when empty.

Members.Name: clear
Members.Doc: Empties the deque; the backing stays allocated, as `List.clear` keeps its.

Items.Name: Map
Items.Doc:
A hash map: open addressing, linear probing, load factor 3/4. The key type says how to
hash and how to compare — `[Hashable<K>]` — and the iteration order is
UNSPECIFIED.

Members.Name: keyColumn
Members.Doc: The key column; `states` says which slots are real.

Members.Name: valueColumn
Members.Doc: The value column, parallel to `keyColumn`.

Members.Name: states
Members.Doc: Per slot: 0 empty, 1 occupied, 2 tombstone.

Members.Name: count
Members.Doc: The occupied slots alone.

Members.Name: used
Members.Doc: Occupied plus tombstones — what the load factor is measured over.

Members.Name: length
Members.Doc: How many values are in it.

Members.Name: isEmpty
Members.Doc: Whether nothing is in it.

Members.Name: empty
Members.Signature: pub static fn empty(): Map<K, V>
Members.Doc: An empty map, with room for the first insertions before a growth.

Members.Name: containsKey
Members.Doc: Whether the key is in the map.

Members.Name: get
Members.Doc: The value for the key, or `null` when the key is absent.

Members.Name: set
Members.Signature: pub mut fn set(key: K, value: V): void
Members.Doc: Inserts, or overwrites the existing entry for an equal key.

Members.Name: getOr
Members.Signature: pub fn getOr(key: K, fallback: V): V
Members.Doc:
The value for the key, or `fallback` when the key is absent — one probe instead of a
`containsKey` before every `get`.

Members.Name: getOrInsert
Members.Signature: pub mut fn getOrInsert(key: K, make: fn() -> V): V
Members.Doc:
The value for the key, inserting what `make` produces first when the key is absent —
`groups.getOrInsert(k, () => List<string>.empty()).push(v)` is the whole of a group-by.
`make` runs only on a miss.

Members.Name: update
Members.Signature: pub mut fn update(key: K, f: fn(?V) -> V): void
Members.Doc:
Replaces the value for the key with what `f` makes of the current one — `null` when the
key is absent — and stores the answer: `counts.update(word, (n) => (n ?? 0) + 1)`.

Members.Name: keys
Members.Doc: A fresh cursor over the keys; the order follows the hashes and is UNSPECIFIED.

Members.Name: values
Members.Doc: A fresh cursor over the values, in the same unspecified order as `keys`.

Members.Name: entries
Members.Doc: A fresh cursor over `(key, value)` pairs: `for (entry in m.entries()) { let (k, v) = entry; … }`.

Members.Name: fromEntries
Members.Signature: pub static fn fromEntries(pairs: (K, V)[]): Map<K, V>
Members.Doc: A map from `(key, value)` pairs; a later pair with an equal key overwrites, as `set`.

Members.Name: capacity
Members.Doc:
How many slots the table holds, empty ones included — what the map costs; `length` is
the truth for everything else.

Members.Name: clear
Members.Doc:
Empties the map. The backing arrays are KEPT, as in `List.clear`; the tombstones vanish
with everything else.

Members.Name: remove
Members.Doc: Removes and returns the old value, or `null` when the key was absent.

Items.Name: sortList
Items.Doc: Sorts in place by the natural order of the type.

Items.Name: sortListBy
Items.Signature: pub fn sortListBy<T>(xs: List<T>, less: fn(T, T) -> bool): void
Items.Doc:
Sorts in place with a comparison of your own.

`less(a, b)` must return `true` when `a` comes STRICTLY before `b`. A `less` returning `true`
for equal elements destroys stability; a contradictory `less` makes the output arbitrary but
crashes nothing, because the algorithm only compares.

Items.Name: Set
Items.Doc:
A hash set: the same probing as `Map`, without the value column. Iteration order is
UNSPECIFIED. `Iterable`, so `for (v in set)` walks it directly.

Members.Name: items
Members.Doc: The element column; `states` says which slots are real.

Members.Name: states
Members.Doc: Per slot: 0 empty, 1 occupied, 2 tombstone.

Members.Name: count
Members.Doc: The occupied slots alone.

Members.Name: used
Members.Doc: Occupied plus tombstones — what the load factor is measured over.

Members.Name: length
Members.Doc: How many values are in it.

Members.Name: isEmpty
Members.Doc: Whether nothing is in it.

Members.Name: of
Members.Signature: pub static fn of(items: T[]): Set<T>
Members.Doc: A set holding the elements of an array: `Set<int>.of([3, 1, 3])` has two elements.

Members.Name: addAll
Members.Signature: pub mut fn addAll(items: T[]): int
Members.Doc: Adds every element of the array; answers how many were new.

Members.Name: toArray
Members.Doc: The elements as an array, in the unspecified order of the walk.

Members.Name: toList
Members.Doc: The elements as a list, in the unspecified order of the walk.

Members.Name: empty
Members.Doc: An empty set.

Members.Name: contains
Members.Doc: Whether the value is in the set.

Members.Name: add
Members.Signature: pub mut fn add(value: T): bool
Members.Doc:
Adds and returns `true` when the value was NEW.

The return value saves a preceding `contains`, which would probe twice.

Members.Name: remove
Members.Signature: pub mut fn remove(value: T): bool
Members.Doc: Removes and returns `true` when the value was present.

Members.Name: clear
Members.Doc:
Empties the set. The backing arrays are KEPT, as in `List.clear`; the tombstones vanish
with everything else.

Members.Name: iter
Members.Doc: A fresh cursor on every call.

Items.Name: SetIterator
Items.Doc:
Walks the occupied slots. The order follows the hashes and is therefore UNSPECIFIED; a
caller that needs one sorts.

Members.Name: source
Members.Doc: The set being walked.

Members.Name: index
Members.Doc: The next slot to look at.

Members.Name: next
Members.Doc: The next value, or `null` at the end.

Items.Name: union
Items.Signature: pub fn union<T :: [Hashable<T>]>(a: Set<T>, b: Set<T>): Set<T>
Items.Doc: Everything in either set, as a NEW set; neither argument changes.

Items.Name: intersect
Items.Signature: pub fn intersect<T :: [Hashable<T>]>(a: Set<T>, b: Set<T>): Set<T>
Items.Doc: Everything in both sets, as a NEW set; neither argument changes.

Items.Name: difference
Items.Signature: pub fn difference<T :: [Hashable<T>]>(a: Set<T>, b: Set<T>): Set<T>
Items.Doc: Everything in `a` that is not in `b`, as a NEW set; neither argument changes.

Items.Name: isSubset
Items.Signature: pub fn isSubset<T :: [Hashable<T>]>(a: Set<T>, b: Set<T>): bool
Items.Doc: Whether every element of `a` is in `b`.

Items.Name: MapKeyIterator
Items.Doc: Walks the keys; the order follows the hashes and is UNSPECIFIED.

Members.Name: source
Members.Doc: The map being walked.

Members.Name: index
Members.Doc: The next slot to look at.

Members.Name: next
Members.Doc: The next key, or `null` at the end.

Items.Name: MapValueIterator
Items.Doc: Walks the values; the order follows the hashes and is UNSPECIFIED.

Members.Name: source
Members.Doc: The map being walked.

Members.Name: index
Members.Doc: The next slot to look at.

Members.Name: next
Members.Doc: The next value, or `null` at the end.

Items.Name: MapEntryIterator
Items.Doc:
Walks key and value TOGETHER; the order follows the hashes and is UNSPECIFIED.

Without this, walking both meant iterating `keys` and paying a second probe per key
through `get`.

Members.Name: source
Members.Doc: The map being walked.

Members.Name: index
Members.Doc: The next slot to look at.

Members.Name: next
Members.Doc: The next `(key, value)` pair, or `null` at the end.

Items.Name: keys
Items.Signature: pub fn keys<K :: [Hashable<K>], V>(m: Map<K, V>): Iterator<K>
Items.Doc: A fresh cursor over the keys.

Items.Name: values
Items.Signature: pub fn values<K :: [Hashable<K>], V>(m: Map<K, V>): Iterator<V>
Items.Doc: A fresh cursor over the values.

Items.Name: entries
Items.Signature: pub fn entries<K :: [Hashable<K>], V>(m: Map<K, V>): Iterator<(K, V)>
Items.Doc:
A fresh cursor over `(key, value)` pairs:

    for (entry in entries(m)) { let (k, v) = entry; … }

Items.Name: arrayOf
Items.Signature: pub fn arrayOf<T>(n: int, f: fn(int) -> T): T[]
Items.Doc:
An array of `n` values, the one at position `i` being `f(i)`: `arrayOf(3, (i) => i * i)`
is `[0, 1, 4]`. `f` runs once per slot, in order, and never for `n <= 0`, which answers
the empty array.

Items.Name: arrayFilled
Items.Signature: pub fn arrayFilled<T>(n: int, value: T): T[]
Items.Doc:
`n` copies of `value` — `[value] * n`, except that `n <= 0` answers the empty array
without an element to write down.

Items.Name: mapList
Items.Signature: pub fn mapList<T, U>(xs: List<T>, f: fn(T) -> U): List<U>
Items.Doc:
A new list of `f` applied to every element, EAGERLY: the work happens here, once.
`xs.iter().map(f)` is the lazy form for a chain that goes on.

Items.Name: sortListByKey
Items.Signature: pub fn sortListByKey<T, K :: [Ordered<K>]>(xs: List<T>, key: fn(T) -> K): void
Items.Doc:
Sorts in place by a key of each element: `sortListByKey(people, (p) => p.age)`. Stable, as
every sort here; the key is computed on every comparison, so a costly key wants a `map` to a
tuple first.

Items.Name: sortArray
Items.Doc:
Sorts an array in place by the natural order of the type — through a list, because the
merge sort lives there; the array's own slots receive the result.

Items.Name: maxBy
Items.Signature: pub fn maxBy<T, K :: [Ordered<K>]>(xs: List<T>, key: fn(T) -> K): ?T
Items.Doc: The element with the largest key, or `null` for an empty list; the FIRST one on a tie.

Items.Name: minBy
Items.Signature: pub fn minBy<T, K :: [Ordered<K>]>(xs: List<T>, key: fn(T) -> K): ?T
Items.Doc: The element with the smallest key, or `null` for an empty list; the FIRST one on a tie.

Items.Name: slice
Items.Signature: pub fn slice<T>(xs: T[], from: int, to: int): T[]
Items.Doc:
The elements from `from` up to but not including `to`, as a NEW array — `List.slice`'s
edges: `0 <= from <= to <= length`, anything else a panic.

Items.Name: listRemove
Items.Signature: pub fn listRemove<T :: [Equatable<T>]>(xs: List<T>, value: T): bool
Items.Doc: Removes the FIRST occurrence of `value`, by `equals`; whether one was there.

Items.Name: groupBy
Items.Signature: pub fn groupBy<T, K :: [Hashable<K>]>(xs: List<T>, key: fn(T) -> K): Map<K, List<T>>
Items.Doc:
The elements grouped by a key, in first-seen order within each group. Every step of the
idiom in one place: `groupBy(words, (w) => w.length())`.

Items.Name: listContains
Items.Signature: pub fn listContains<T :: [Equatable<T>]>(xs: List<T>, value: T): bool
Items.Doc: Whether the value occurs, by `equals`; O(n).

Items.Name: listIndexOf
Items.Signature: pub fn listIndexOf<T :: [Equatable<T>]>(xs: List<T>, value: T): ?int
Items.Doc: The position of the first occurrence, or `null` when there is none.

Modules.Doc:
What the language itself needs: aborting with a reason, the ready-made `Throwable`, and the
interfaces the built-in types satisfy.

`panic` and `coroutineEnded` are bound by the compiler, so nothing has to import this module to
reach them.

Items.Name: panic
Items.Doc:
Ends the program with `message` and a backtrace.

Not catchable. Its return type is `never`, so the flow analysis treats everything after a call as
unreachable — which is why `expect` can return a non-optional after panicking.

Items.Name: coroutineEnded
Items.Doc:
Panics because a coroutine was resumed after its body had run to the end.

Called from a dispatcher nobody wrote, which is why nobody could have written the import either.

Items.Name: assert
Items.Signature: pub fn assert(condition: bool, message: string): void
Items.Doc:
Panics with `message` when `condition` is false, for invariants the compiler does not check.

`void` rather than `never`: it does not replace a `return`, and a function ending in `assert` is
still `LYR-SEM0017`.

Items.Name: todo
Items.Doc:
Marks a place that is still missing. Unlike a comment it reports itself when reached, with
`not implemented:` before the message.

Items.Name: unreachable
Items.Doc:
Marks a branch that must never be taken, with `unreachable:` before the message.

`todo` means *still to come*; this means *must never happen*. Reaching it says that an assumption
stated somewhere else is wrong.

Items.Name: Exception
Items.Doc: The ready-made `Throwable` for throwing a message: `throw Exception { text = "…" };`.

Members.Name: text
Members.Doc: What `message()` returns.

Members.Name: message
Members.Doc: The text this exception was built with.

Items.Name: Display
Items.Doc:
What can be rendered as text — the anchor for `print`, `println` and `std.fmt`.

Every built-in scalar satisfies it through an `extend`, and a user type through `::`. A value
held THROUGH the interface (`let d: Display = 5;`) stays rejected: an interface value is a fat
pointer and needs a reference, which a scalar has none of.

Members.Name: show
Members.Doc: This value as text.

Items.Name: Equatable
Items.Doc:
Values of this type can be compared for equality.

Generic rather than `fn equals(other: Equatable)`, so both sides carry the concrete type: an
interface as a parameter type would need an interface VALUE, and a scalar cannot be one — there
would be no `Map<int, V>`.

Members.Name: equals
Members.Doc: Whether the two are equal.

Items.Name: Hashable
Items.Doc:
Values of this type can be hashed, which is what a `Map` key and a `Set` element need.

**Equal values must produce equal hashes.** No compiler checks it and every hash table depends on
it. The reverse does not hold — two different values may collide.

`Hashable<T>` implies `Equatable<T>` (its parent since 2.0): a hash table cannot exist
without equality. A key constraint is `K :: [Hashable<K>]` alone.

Members.Name: hash
Members.Doc: The hash of this value.

Items.Name: Ordered
Items.Doc:
Values of this type have an order — what sorting and range queries need.

One comparison instead of four methods: `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` all derive from it.

Members.Name: compare
Members.Doc:
Negative when this comes first, zero when the two are equal, positive when `other` comes
first — as `strcmp`.

Items.Name: Add
Items.Doc: Values of this type can be added: `a + b` is `a.add(b)`.

Members.Name: add
Members.Doc: The sum of this value and `other`.

Items.Name: Sub
Items.Doc: Values of this type can be subtracted: `a - b` is `a.sub(b)`.

Members.Name: sub
Members.Doc: This value minus `other`.

Items.Name: Mul
Items.Doc: Values of this type can be multiplied: `a * b` is `a.mul(b)`.

Members.Name: mul
Members.Doc: The product of this value and `other`.

Items.Name: Div
Items.Doc: Values of this type can be divided: `a / b` is `a.div(b)`.

Members.Name: div
Members.Doc:
This value divided by `other`. What a division by zero does is the type's own business;
the built-in numerics panic.

Items.Name: Into
Items.Doc:
A value of this type converts to `T`: `x as T` is `x.into()`.

ONE target per type: the method is named `into`, and a type has one member of a name — a second
conversion is an ordinary named method. Total conversions only; a conversion that can fail
belongs in a named function returning an optional.

The numeric casts keep their opcodes: `1 as float` never goes through here.

Members.Name: into
Members.Doc: This value as a `T`.

Items.Name: OnModule
Items.Doc: A struct declaring this may stand as `@Name` before the module header.

Items.Name: OnType
Items.Doc: A struct declaring this may stand as `@Name` before a struct, class or enum declaration.

Items.Name: OnFunction
Items.Doc: A struct declaring this may stand as `@Name` before a top-level function.

Items.Name: WithArg
Items.Doc:
An attribute declaring this takes its one value in parentheses — `@On(Event.Damage)` — and
the value fills the attribute's FIRST field, whose type must be `T`. The braces form stays
open to every attribute; this one is opted into, so a struct's field order never becomes an
argument order by accident.

Items.Name: Deprecated
Items.Doc:
Marks its target as deprecated: the compiler warns at every use, and `message` says what to
use instead. The first attribute the compiler itself reads — it changes diagnostics and
nothing else, so a program that ignores the warning runs unchanged.

Members.Name: message
Members.Doc: What to use instead; shown in the warning at every use site.

Members.Name: until
Members.Doc:
The version this is kept until, as `"3.5"` — and it is a PROMISE the compiler enforces:
building with a toolchain that has reached that version is an error (`LYR-SEM0081`), so
the removal happens because the build stops, not because somebody remembered.

Empty means the ordinary policy: warn now, remove at the next major.

Items.Name: combineHash
Items.Signature: pub fn combineHash(seed: int, value: int): int
Items.Doc:
Folds `value` into `seed` — what a `hash()` over several fields is built from:
`combineHash(combineHash(0, this.x.hash()), this.y.hash())`. Order matters, so `(1, 2)` and
`(2, 1)` differ. The anchor a synthesized `Hashable` conformance (4.5) combines the fields
with, so a hand-written `hash()` and a synthesized one agree.

The formula is Boost's `hash_combine` at 64 bits: the golden-ratio constant keeps a run of
small values from cancelling, and the two shifts spread each field over the whole word.

Items.Name: OnMethod
Items.Doc:
A struct declaring this may stand as `@Name` before a METHOD or a field — the seat a
`@Deprecated` on `List.oldName` needs. An anchor for the compiler (4.5): declared here so a
library can name it today, honoured once the attribute rows carry members.

Items.Name: NonExhaustive
Items.Doc:
Marks an enum as one that may GAIN variants without breaking its callers: a `match` over it
outside the declaring module must carry a `_` arm, so `Wait` or `IoErrorKind` can grow. The
same contract Rust's `#[non_exhaustive]` states. An anchor for the compiler (4.5): the
attribute is data today, the rule follows in the exhaustiveness check.

Items.Name: EncodingError
Items.Doc:
Where and why a text was refused: the 0-based character offset of the refusal, and what the
decoder expected there.

Items.Name: hexEncode
Items.Doc:
Bytes as lowercase hexadecimal, two characters per byte, no separators. Empty bytes are the
empty string.

Items.Name: hexDecode
Items.Doc:
The bytes a hexadecimal string spells, or `null` when it spells none: an odd length or a
character outside `0-9`, `a-f`, `A-F`. The empty string is an empty array.

Items.Name: hexDecodeOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn hexDecodeOrThrow(text: string): uint8[] throws EncodingError
Items.Doc:
`hexDecode`, with the reason when the text spells no bytes: where it broke, and what a
hexadecimal string would have had there.

Items.Name: hexDecodeOrErr
Items.Signature: pub fn hexDecodeOrErr(text: string): Result<uint8[], EncodingError>
Items.Doc:
`hexDecode`, with the reason as a VALUE: the bytes, or the `EncodingError` that
`hexDecodeOrThrow` would throw.

Items.Name: base64Encode
Items.Doc:
Bytes as base64 (RFC 4648 §4: `A-Za-z0-9+/`), padded with `=` to a multiple of four
characters. Empty bytes are the empty string.

Items.Name: base64Decode
Items.Doc:
The bytes a base64 string spells, or `null` when it spells none. Strict: the length must be a
multiple of four, `=` may appear only as the final one or two characters, characters outside
the alphabet are refused, and so is padding whose unused bits are not zero — accepted input is
exactly what `base64Encode` produces. The empty string is an empty array.

Items.Name: base64DecodeOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn base64DecodeOrThrow(text: string): uint8[] throws EncodingError
Items.Doc:
`base64Decode`, with the reason when the text spells no bytes: where it broke, and what a
base64 string would have had there.

Items.Name: formatInt
Items.Signature: pub fn formatInt(value: int, spec: string): string
Items.Doc:
An `int` through a .NET numeric specifier (`N0`, `D5`, `X`, ...). An invalid specifier is a
panic rather than an error value: it is a literal in the source and does not depend on the
input.

`X` renders the BITS: `formatInt(-255, "X")` is the two's complement
`FFFFFFFFFFFFFF01`, as `{:x}` in Rust and `%x` in Go write it. `formatHex` renders the
VALUE with a sign, `-ff`, as Python's `hex` does; which one a program wants depends on
whether the number is a quantity or a bit pattern, and each name says which it gives.

Items.Name: formatUint
Items.Signature: pub fn formatUint(value: uint, spec: string): string
Items.Doc: A `uint` through a .NET numeric specifier; large values stay positive.

Items.Name: formatFloat
Items.Signature: pub fn formatFloat(value: float, spec: string): string
Items.Doc: A `float` through a .NET numeric specifier (`N2`, `F3`, `E2`, `P1`, ...).

Items.Name: formatBool
Items.Signature: pub fn formatBool(value: bool, spec: string): string
Items.Doc: A `bool` through a .NET specifier.

Items.Name: formatChar
Items.Signature: pub fn formatChar(value: char, spec: string): string
Items.Doc: A `char` through a .NET specifier.

Items.Name: formatString
Items.Signature: pub fn formatString(value: string, spec: string): string
Items.Doc:
A string at a width: padding on the right (`{name:10}`) or, with a leading minus, on the
left (`{name:-10}`).

Items.Name: formatRadix
Items.Signature: pub fn formatRadix(value: int, radix: int): string
Items.Doc:
To a base from 2 to 36. Letters from `a` for digit values above 9.

The inverse of `std.string.parseIntRadix`. They live in different modules because parsing is
text processing and formatting is output, and `std.string` must not import `std.fmt`.

Items.Name: formatHex
Items.Doc:
Hexadecimal, lower case, no prefix — the VALUE, so a negative number carries a sign:
`formatHex(-255)` is `-ff`. The bit pattern is `formatInt(value, "x")`.

Items.Name: formatBinary
Items.Doc: Binary, no prefix.

Items.Name: formatOctal
Items.Doc: Octal, no prefix.

Items.Name: formatHexPadded
Items.Signature: pub fn formatHexPadded(value: int, width: int): string
Items.Doc:
Hexadecimal with a fixed number of digits and leading zeros: `formatHexPadded(255, 4)` is
`"00ff"`, for addresses and colour values where the width carries meaning.

Items.Name: padLeft
Items.Signature: pub fn padLeft(value: string, width: int): string
Items.Doc: Pads with spaces at the FRONT until `width` is reached; longer strings stay unchanged.

Items.Name: padRight
Items.Signature: pub fn padRight(value: string, width: int): string
Items.Doc: Pads with spaces at the END until `width` is reached; longer strings stay unchanged.

Items.Name: center
Items.Signature: pub fn center(value: string, width: int): string
Items.Doc:
Centres. On an odd remainder the extra character goes to the RIGHT.
A decision rather than a matter of course, but without it the same input yields two different
results depending on the implementation.

Items.Name: formatBytes
Items.Doc:
Bytes in readable form: `1536` becomes `"1.5 KB"`.

Base 1024 with the prefixes without `i` (`KB` rather than `KiB`), the spelling operating
systems and tools actually use.

Items.Name: table
Items.Signature: pub fn table(rows: string[][], separator: string): string
Items.Doc:
Aligns columns. Each row is a `string[]`; short rows are padded with empty cells.

No borders and no header handling: what a table means is the caller's business. This does the
tedious part — two passes over the data, to know the column widths before printing.

Modules.Doc:
Digests and checksums over bytes: `sha256`, `sha1`, `md5` and `crc32`, plus the hex
conveniences over text and `hashCombine` for a `Hashable` built from several fields.

Items.Name: sha256
Items.Doc:
The SHA-256 digest: 32 bytes. The one to reach for when the digest must resist an
attacker — content addressing, integrity checks, tokens derived from secrets.

Items.Name: sha1
Items.Doc:
The SHA-1 digest: 20 bytes. Broken for collision resistance since 2017; here because git
and older protocols still speak it, not for anything new.

Items.Name: md5
Items.Doc: The MD5 digest: 16 bytes. Broken; here for legacy checksums and for nothing else.

Items.Name: crc32
Items.Doc:
The CRC-32 checksum (IEEE 802.3, the polynomial zip, PNG and Ethernet use), as a
non-negative `int` below 2^32. Detects accidental corruption; a deliberate change is
trivially hidden from it.

Items.Name: sha256Hex
Items.Doc:
`sha256` over the UTF-8 bytes of `text`, as lower-case hex — the form a checksum file or a
content id is written in.

Items.Name: sha1Hex
Items.Doc: `sha1` over the UTF-8 bytes of `text`, as lower-case hex.

Items.Name: md5Hex
Items.Doc: `md5` over the UTF-8 bytes of `text`, as lower-case hex.

Items.Name: hashCombine
Items.Signature: pub fn hashCombine(seed: int, value: int): int
Items.Doc:
Folds `value` into `seed`, for a `hash()` over several fields:
`hashCombine(hashCombine(0, this.x.hash()), this.y.hash())`. Order matters, so `(1, 2)`
and `(2, 1)` hash differently. The same function as `std.core.combineHash`, named here
beside the digests.

Items.Name: hashAll
Items.Doc: The hash of a whole array of hashes, folded in order from a seed of zero.

Modules.Doc:
Reading from and writing to the console.

Output needs no capability — it is always available. `print` and `println` take any type that
satisfies `Display`: `println(42)`, `println(true)`, `println("hi")`.

Items.Name: print
Items.Doc:
Writes any displayable value without a line break: `print(42)`, `print("hi")`.

There is no overloading; the `Display` constraint does the same job and extends to every type
that satisfies it rather than to a fixed list. Monomorphization turns the call into a direct one
per used type, so the generality costs nothing at runtime.

Nothing is flushed. A prompt written with `print` sits in the buffer until `flush`, which is why
`prompt` exists.

Items.Name: println
Items.Doc: Writes any displayable value, followed by a line break.

Items.Name: eprint
Items.Doc: Writes any displayable value to standard ERROR without a line break.

Items.Name: eprintln
Items.Doc:
Writes any displayable value to standard ERROR, followed by a line break.

Diagnostics belong here rather than in standard output, so a program used in a pipe does not put
them into the data.

Items.Name: readLine
Items.Doc:
Reads one line from standard input, without its line break.

`null` at end of input. Optional rather than an empty string, because EOF is a state and not a
line: a program reading until `null` stops, one reading until `""` never does.

Items.Name: readAll
Items.Doc:
Reads everything up to end of input, for filters that need the whole text.

The input is held in memory in full. `lines` is the way through a stream larger than that.

Items.Name: readChar
Items.Doc: Reads a single code point, or `null` at end of input.

Items.Name: isInteractive
Items.Doc:
Whether standard input and output are a terminal rather than a pipe.

A program writing into a pipe should not put a prompt into the stream, and this is how it knows.

Items.Name: flush
Items.Doc:
Pushes buffered output to the console.

Needed as soon as something is written without a line break and has to be visible before the
program continues — a prompt being the usual case.

Items.Name: prompt
Items.Doc:
Writes `text`, flushes it, and reads one line.

The flush is the point: without it the question would sit in the buffer while the program waits
for an answer nobody knows is expected. `null` at end of input, as `readLine`.

Items.Name: LineIterator
Items.Doc: The iterator `lines` hands out. Yields each line of standard input until it ends.

Members.Name: done
Members.Doc: Set once `readLine` answered `null`; from then on the iterator ends.

Members.Name: next
Members.Doc: The next line, or `null` once the input has ended. Ends for good after the first `null`.

Items.Name: lines
Items.Doc:
The lines of standard input, as an iterator — the idiomatic shape of a filter:

    for (line in console.lines()) { … }

An iterator rather than a `string[]`: the input can be larger than memory, and a program that
only counts should not have to collect it first.

Items.Name: IoErrorKind
Items.Doc:
What went wrong, as a matchable name. `Other` carries everything the platform reports that
has no name here — a locked file, a full disk — and the `detail` string still says it.
Only kinds every platform can CLASSIFY reliably get a name; the carrier-plus-kind shape is
what lets this list grow later without breaking anyone's `match`.

Members.Name: ConnectionRefused
Members.Doc: The peer answered "no" — nothing listens there (4.0, with `std.io.net`).

Members.Name: AddressInUse
Members.Doc: The local address is already taken (4.0, with `std.io.net`).

Items.Name: IoError
Items.Doc:
The reason an I/O operation failed: which kind, on which path, and what the platform said.

§9.0's answer to "why not?" — the silent forms (`text`, `writeText`, …) answer only whether.

Items.Name: text
Items.Doc:
The whole content as text, decoded as UTF-8 — bytes that are not valid UTF-8 become
U+FFFD. For binary data use `bytes`. `null` when the file does not exist or is not readable.

Items.Name: bytes
Items.Doc:
The raw bytes, undecoded — what `text` cannot give: its UTF-8 decoding turns invalid bytes
into U+FFFD. `null` when the file is not readable; an EMPTY array is an empty file.

Items.Name: lines
Items.Doc:
The lines of a file, terminators removed, so whether the file used CRLF or LF is no longer
visible. `null` when the file is not readable; an EMPTY array is an empty file.

Items.Name: writeText
Items.Signature: pub fn writeText(path: string, content: string): bool
Items.Doc: Writes text (UTF-8), replacing an existing file. `true` on success.

Items.Name: appendText
Items.Signature: pub fn appendText(path: string, content: string): bool
Items.Doc: Appends to an existing file or creates it. `true` on success.

Items.Name: exists
Items.Doc: Whether something — file or directory — exists at the path.

Items.Name: remove
Items.Doc: `true` when the file is gone afterwards, including when it never existed.

Items.Name: writeBytes
Items.Signature: pub fn writeBytes(path: string, data: uint8[]): bool
Items.Doc:
Writes raw bytes, replacing an existing file. `true` on success — the `writeText`
convention. (v1.14: the first native whose parameter is an array.)

Items.Name: appendBytes
Items.Signature: pub fn appendBytes(path: string, data: uint8[]): bool
Items.Doc: Appends raw bytes to an existing file or creates it. `true` on success.

Items.Name: textOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn textOrThrow(path: string): string throws IoError
Items.Doc: `text`, with the reason when it cannot: the content, or an `IoError` saying why not.

Items.Name: textOrErr
Items.Signature: pub fn textOrErr(path: string): Result<string, IoError>
Items.Doc:
`text`, with the reason as a VALUE: the content, or the `IoError` that `textOrThrow`
would throw — for a read whose failure is stored or handled later rather than caught here.

Items.Name: bytesOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn bytesOrThrow(path: string): uint8[] throws IoError
Items.Doc: `bytes`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: linesOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn linesOrThrow(path: string): string[] throws IoError
Items.Doc: `lines`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: sizeOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn sizeOrThrow(path: string): int throws IoError
Items.Doc: `size`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: entriesOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn entriesOrThrow(path: string): string[] throws IoError
Items.Doc: `entries`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: writeTextOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn writeTextOrThrow(path: string, content: string): void throws IoError
Items.Doc: `writeText`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: appendTextOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn appendTextOrThrow(path: string, content: string): void throws IoError
Items.Doc: `appendText`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: writeBytesOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn writeBytesOrThrow(path: string, data: uint8[]): void throws IoError
Items.Doc: `writeBytes`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: appendBytesOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn appendBytesOrThrow(path: string, data: uint8[]): void throws IoError
Items.Doc: `appendBytes`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: removeOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn removeOrThrow(path: string): void throws IoError
Items.Doc:
`remove`, with the reason when it cannot. A file that never existed is still success, as in
`remove` — the twin throws exactly where the silent form answers `false`.

Items.Name: copyOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn copyOrThrow(from: string, to: string): void throws IoError
Items.Doc: `copy`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: moveOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn moveOrThrow(from: string, to: string): void throws IoError
Items.Doc: `move`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: createDirOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn createDirOrThrow(path: string): void throws IoError
Items.Doc: `createDir`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: createDirAllOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn createDirAllOrThrow(path: string): void throws IoError
Items.Doc: `createDirAll`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: removeDirOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn removeDirOrThrow(path: string): void throws IoError
Items.Doc: `removeDir`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: size
Items.Doc: The size in bytes, or `null` when the file does not exist.

Items.Name: modifiedMillis
Items.Doc:
When the file was last written, as milliseconds since the Unix epoch (UTC), or `null` when
it does not exist — what a watcher compares between two looks without reading the content.
Milliseconds rather than an `Instant`, because `std.time` costs `osAccess` and a file
module must not; `Instant.ofEpochMillis` turns it into one.

Items.Name: isFile
Items.Doc: Whether the path names an existing FILE.

Items.Name: isDirectory
Items.Doc: Whether the path names an existing DIRECTORY.

Items.Name: copy
Items.Signature: pub fn copy(from: string, to: string): bool
Items.Doc: Copies. `false` when the source is missing or the target is not writable.

Items.Name: move
Items.Signature: pub fn move(from: string, to: string): bool
Items.Doc: Moves or renames; the same operation on every file system.

Items.Name: createDir
Items.Doc: Creates one directory; the parent must exist. `createDirAll` creates the chain.

Items.Name: createDirAll
Items.Doc: Creates missing parent directories too. An existing directory counts as success.

Items.Name: removeDir
Items.Doc:
Deletes an EMPTY directory. There is no recursive delete; a caller that needs one writes
the loop visibly.

Items.Name: entries
Items.Doc:
The entries of a directory: names rather than paths, sorted alphabetically. `null` when the
directory cannot be read; an EMPTY array is an empty directory — the 2.14 convention, which
`listDir` predates.

Items.Name: tempDir
Items.Doc: A path in the system's temporary directory. Does NOT create the file.

Modules.Doc:
TCP for tasks: `listen`/`accept` on the server side, `connect` on the client's,
`readSome`/`write` on both, every waiting form yielding to the scheduler instead of
blocking the thread.

The silent forms answer *whether* (`null`/`false`); the `OrThrow` twins say *why* with an
`IoError`, from the same implementation. `readSome` folds three truths into one answer:
bytes are bytes, an EMPTY array is the peer being done (EOF), and `null` is a failure.

Items.Name: Listener
Items.Doc: A listening endpoint. Opaque: it is issued here, never assembled.

Items.Name: Socket
Items.Doc: A connected stream. Opaque, like the listener.

Items.Name: UdpSocket
Items.Doc: A UDP endpoint. Opaque, like the others; one handle both sends and receives.

Items.Name: Packet
Items.Doc:
One received datagram: its payload, and who sent it — the address `sendTo` answers to.

UDP has no EOF, so an EMPTY payload here is a real (empty) packet, not an end — the one
place this module's bytes mean something different than `readSome`'s.

Members.Name: bytes
Members.Doc: The payload, complete: a datagram arrives whole or not at all.

Members.Name: host
Members.Doc: The sender's address, as the receiving socket saw it.

Members.Name: port
Members.Doc: The sender's port.

Items.Name: listen
Items.Signature: pub fn listen(host: string, port: int): ?Listener
Items.Doc:
Listens on `host:port`. Port 0 asks the OS for a free one — `localPort` says which.
`null` when the address cannot be taken; `listenOrThrow` says why.

Items.Name: listenOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn listenOrThrow(host: string, port: int): Listener throws IoError
Items.Doc: `listen`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: localPort
Items.Doc: The port a listener actually holds — the answer to `listen(host, 0)`.

Items.Name: accept
Items.Doc: Waits for the next connection. `null` when the listener broke; `acceptOrThrow` says why.

Items.Name: acceptOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn acceptOrThrow(listener: Listener): Socket throws IoError
Items.Doc: `accept`, with the reason when the listener broke.

Items.Name: connect
Items.Signature: pub fn connect(host: string, port: int): ?Socket
Items.Doc:
Waits until a connection to `host:port` stands or is refused. `null` on refusal or any
other failure; `connectOrThrow` names the kind — `ConnectionRefused` when nothing listens.

Items.Name: connectOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn connectOrThrow(host: string, port: int): Socket throws IoError
Items.Doc: `connect`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: readSome
Items.Signature: pub fn readSome(socket: Socket, max: int): ?uint8[]
Items.Doc:
Waits for bytes and reads up to `max` of them. Three truths in one answer: bytes are
bytes, an EMPTY array is the peer being done (EOF), and `null` is a failure —
`readSomeOrThrow` says which failure.

A `max` of zero or less PANICS: an empty answer already means EOF, so there is no
honest value to hand back for it.

Items.Name: readSomeOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn readSomeOrThrow(socket: Socket, max: int): uint8[] throws IoError
Items.Doc:
`readSome`, with the reason when the stream broke. EOF stays the empty array — the peer
being done is an ordinary state, not a failure.

Items.Name: write
Items.Signature: pub fn write(socket: Socket, bytes: uint8[]): bool
Items.Doc:
Writes ALL of `bytes`, waiting whenever the stream is full. `false` when the stream broke
midway; `writeOrThrow` says why.

Items.Name: writeOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn writeOrThrow(socket: Socket, bytes: uint8[]): void throws IoError
Items.Doc: `write`, with the reason when the stream broke.

Items.Name: close
Items.Doc: Closes a socket. Closing twice closes once.

Items.Name: closeListener
Items.Doc: Closes a listener.

Items.Name: bind
Items.Signature: pub fn bind(host: string, port: int): ?UdpSocket
Items.Doc:
Binds a UDP endpoint on `host:port`. Port 0 asks the OS for a free one — `localPort` says
which. `null` when the address cannot be taken; `bindOrThrow` says why, `AddressInUse`
being the usual answer.

Items.Name: bindOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn bindOrThrow(host: string, port: int): UdpSocket throws IoError
Items.Doc: `bind`, with the reason when it cannot.

Items.Name: localPort
Items.Doc: The port a UDP endpoint actually holds — the answer to `bind(host, 0)`.

Items.Name: sendTo
Items.Signature: pub fn sendTo(socket: UdpSocket, host: string, port: int, bytes: uint8[]): bool
Items.Doc:
Sends one datagram to `host:port`, waiting out a full send buffer. The datagram goes
whole or not at all; `false` when it cannot go — `sendToOrThrow` says why. There is no
delivery promise: that is UDP, not this module.

Items.Name: sendToOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn sendToOrThrow(socket: UdpSocket, host: string, port: int, bytes: uint8[]): void throws IoError
Items.Doc: `sendTo`, with the reason when the datagram cannot go.

Items.Name: receiveFrom
Items.Signature: pub fn receiveFrom(socket: UdpSocket, max: int): ?Packet
Items.Doc:
Waits for one datagram and answers it whole, with its sender. A payload longer than `max`
is CUT to it — datagrams do not queue their remainder. `null` is a failure;
`receiveFromOrThrow` says which. An empty payload is a real packet: UDP has no EOF.

A `max` of zero or less PANICS. It would otherwise cut the datagram to one byte and
throw the rest away, which is the cutting rule above turned into silent data loss.

Items.Name: readSome
Items.Signature: pub fn readSome(file: File, max: int): ?uint8[]
Items.Doc:
Reads up to `max` bytes, waiting for them. Three truths in one answer, the 2.14 convention
`std.io.net` and `std.process` also speak: bytes are bytes, an EMPTY array is the end of the
file, and `null` is a failure — `readSomeOrThrow` says which.

Fewer than `max` bytes is an ordinary answer; call again until the empty array. A `max`
of zero or less PANICS: an empty answer already means the end of the file, so there is
no honest value to hand back for it.

Yields while the read is outstanding, so it needs a running `std.task.run()`.

Items.Doc: `readSome`, with the reason when the read failed. The end of the file stays the empty array.

Items.Signature: pub fn write(file: File, bytes: uint8[]): bool
Items.Doc:
Writes `bytes` and waits for them to land. `false` when the write failed — `writeOrThrow`
says why.

The answer is the OUTCOME, not the handover: a queued write could not report a full disk at
the call, and for a file that is the answer that matters. `std.process` queues its writes for
the opposite reason — a child that reads slowly must not stall its writer.

Yields while the write is outstanding, so it needs a running `std.task.run()`.

Items.Doc: `write`, with the reason when it failed.

"the end", which means a read FAILURE and the end of the file look the same from `next()`
alone — ask `failed()` after the walk when the difference matters.

Every step may yield, so a walk needs a running `std.task.run()`.

because a closure is too much ceremony for counting.

It takes an ARRAY rather than an iterator, and that is not a convenience. An
`Iterator<?T>` cannot exist: `next()` answers `?T` and spends `null` on "the end", so an
optional element would need `??T` to be told apart from it, and `?` does not nest. Reading the
slots directly is what makes the distinction available at all.

Items.Doc: The tangent of an angle in radians.

Items.Name: log
Items.Doc: The natural logarithm; `logBase` covers every other base.

Items.Name: asin
Items.Doc: The inverse sine, in radians. Outside `[-1, 1]` the result is NaN.

Items.Name: acos
Items.Doc: The inverse cosine, in radians. Outside `[-1, 1]` the result is NaN.

Items.Name: atan
Items.Doc: The inverse tangent, in radians.

Items.Name: atan2
Items.Signature: pub fn atan2(y: float, x: float): float
Items.Doc: The angle of the point `(x, y)` in radians — the quadrant-aware inverse tangent.

Items.Name: tau
Items.Doc: The full turn: 2π.

Items.Name: intMax
Items.Doc: The largest `int`, 2^63 - 1.

Items.Name: intMin
Items.Doc:
The smallest `int`, -2^63. It has no positive twin: `absInt(intMin)` is `intMin` again, and
`0 - intMin` too — arithmetic wraps.

Items.Name: absInt
Items.Doc:
The absolute value. The most negative `int` has no positive twin and comes back
unchanged — arithmetic wraps; `checkedAbs` answers `null` there instead.

Items.Name: checkedAdd
Items.Signature: pub fn checkedAdd(a: int, b: int): ?int
Items.Doc: `a + b`, or `null` when the sum does not fit `int`.

Items.Name: checkedSub

Items.Name: checkedMul

Items.Doc: `a * b`, or `null` when the product does not fit `int`.

Items.Name: checkedAbs
Items.Doc: The absolute value, or `null` for `intMin`, the one value without one.

Items.Name: saturatingAdd
Items.Signature: pub fn saturatingAdd(a: int, b: int): int
Items.Doc: `a + b`, held at `intMax` or `intMin` instead of wrapping.

Items.Name: saturatingSub

Items.Doc: `a - b`, held at the bounds instead of wrapping.

Items.Name: saturatingMul
Items.Signature: pub fn saturatingMul(a: int, b: int): int

Items.Name: minInt
Items.Signature: pub fn minInt(a: int, b: int): int
Items.Doc: The smaller of the two.

Items.Name: maxInt
Items.Signature: pub fn maxInt(a: int, b: int): int
Items.Doc: The larger of the two.

Items.Name: clampInt
Items.Signature: pub fn clampInt(value: int, lo: int, hi: int): int
Items.Doc: Clamps to `[lo, hi]`. A `lo > hi` yields `lo`; the bounds are the caller's business.

Items.Name: signInt
Items.Doc: `-1`, `0` or `1`, matching the sign.

Items.Name: gcd
Items.Signature: pub fn gcd(a: int, b: int): int
Items.Doc: Greatest common divisor, Euclidean. Always non-negative.

Items.Name: lcm
Items.Signature: pub fn lcm(a: int, b: int): int
Items.Doc: Least common multiple. `lcm(0, n)` is 0.

Items.Name: powInt
Items.Signature: pub fn powInt(base: int, exponent: int): ?int
Items.Doc:
Integer power by repeated squaring.

`null` for a negative exponent — the result would be a fraction — and since 4.5 for a result
beyond `int`, which used to wrap silently: `powInt(2, 64)` answered 0.

Items.Name: divFloor
Items.Signature: pub fn divFloor(a: int, b: int): int
Items.Doc:
Division rounding towards negative infinity rather than towards zero.

`/` and `%` follow the sign of the dividend, so `-7 / 2` is -3.
Computing on a grid (tiles, time windows) needs -4. Both forms stand side by side so the
choice is visible.

Items.Name: modFloor
Items.Signature: pub fn modFloor(a: int, b: int): int
Items.Doc: The remainder matching `divFloor`, always carrying the sign of `b`.

Items.Name: clamp
Items.Signature: pub fn clamp(value: float, lo: float, hi: float): float
Items.Doc: Clamps to `[lo, hi]`. A `lo > hi` yields `lo`; the bounds are the caller's business.

Items.Name: sign
Items.Doc: `-1.0`, `0.0` or `1.0`, matching the sign. NaN yields `0.0`.

Items.Name: trunc
Items.Doc: Truncates towards zero: `trunc(-2.7)` is `-2.0`, while `floor(-2.7)` would be `-3.0`.

Items.Name: isNaN
Items.Doc:
`NaN` is the only value unequal to itself (IEEE 754), so this needs no native edge and no bit
access.

Items.Name: isInfinite
Items.Doc: Whether the value is positive or negative infinity. NaN is neither.

Items.Name: isFinite
Items.Doc: Whether the value is neither NaN nor infinite.

Items.Name: exp
Items.Doc: `e` raised to `value`.

Items.Name: log2

Items.Name: log10
Items.Doc: The base-10 logarithm.

Items.Signature: pub fn logBase(value: float, base: float): float
Items.Doc: The logarithm to an arbitrary base.

Items.Name: cbrt
Items.Doc:
The cube root, negative values included.

`pow(x, 1/3)` alone yields NaN for negative `x`: a fractional power is undefined there. The
cube root is not, and the sign simply moves out.

Items.Name: hypot
Items.Signature: pub fn hypot(a: float, b: float): float
Items.Doc: The length of the hypotenuse.

Items.Name: sinh
Items.Doc: The hyperbolic sine.

Items.Name: cosh
Items.Doc: The hyperbolic cosine.

Items.Doc: The hyperbolic tangent.
