Items.Doc: Radians to degrees.

Modules.Doc:
Computing with `?T` without testing first.

There is no `Option<T>` here — `?T` is it, and these are functions over the built-in type.
Absent on purpose, because the language already has them: `unwrap` is `o!`, `unwrapOr` is
`o ?? fallback`, and `isSome`/`isNone` are `o != null`/`o == null`, which is what flow narrowing
keys on. A function would cut that off: after `if (isSome(o))`, `o` would still be a `?T`.

Items.Name: map
Items.Signature: pub fn map<T, U>(o: ?T, f: fn(T) -> U): ?U
Items.Doc: Applies `f` to the value when there is one, and answers `null` when there is not.

Items.Name: andThen
Items.Signature: pub fn andThen<T, U>(o: ?T, f: fn(T) -> ?U): ?U
Items.Doc:
As `map`, but `f` may itself come back empty.

This takes the place of `flatten`: a `map` whose `f` returned `?U` would produce a `??U`, which
is not a type. Here `f` already returns `?U` and the result is that same `?U`.

Items.Name: filter
Items.Signature: pub fn filter<T>(o: ?T, pred: fn(T) -> bool): ?T
Items.Doc: Keeps the value only when `pred` accepts it, and answers `null` otherwise.

Items.Name: zip
Items.Signature: pub fn zip<T, U>(a: ?T, b: ?U): ?(T, U)
Items.Doc:
Both present yields a tuple, otherwise `null`.

The result is taken apart with `let (a, b) = …`.

Items.Name: contains
Items.Signature: pub fn contains<T :: [Equatable<T>]>(o: ?T, value: T): bool
Items.Doc: Whether a value is present and equals `value`.

Items.Name: toArray
Items.Doc: Zero or one element — the bridge to anything that takes an array.

Items.Name: OptionIterator
Items.Doc: The iterator `iter` hands out: yields the value once, if there is one.

Members.Name: value
Members.Doc: The single value, if it was there.

Members.Name: done
Members.Doc: Whether the single value was already yielded.

Members.Name: next
Members.Doc: The value on the first call, `null` on every one after it.

Items.Name: iter
Items.Doc:
An iterator over zero or one value.

Every adapter in `std.iter` then works on an optional, without `std.iter` knowing anything about
`?T`.

Items.Name: expect
Items.Signature: pub fn expect<T>(o: ?T, message: string): T
Items.Doc:
The value, or a panic carrying `message`.

As `o!`, but with a message of your own: `LYR-VM0007` reports that a value was missing, never
which one.

Items.Name: platform
Items.Doc: `"windows"`, `"linux"`, `"macos"` or `"unknown"`.

Items.Name: env
Items.Doc:
An environment variable, or `null` when it is not set — an ordinary question about the
environment, not a panic.

Items.Name: currentDir
Items.Doc: The current working directory.

Items.Name: exit
Items.Doc:
Ends the process immediately with this code. No `defer` runs and no `catch` applies. To
exit cleanly, return from `main`.

Items.Name: args
Items.Doc:
The command-line arguments, also outside `main`.

`main(args)` receives them, but a function deeper in the program does not; here they are
available without threading them through.

Items.Name: setEnv
Items.Signature: pub fn setEnv(name: string, value: string): bool
Items.Doc:
Sets an environment variable for this process. Child processes inherit it; the system does
not.

Items.Name: hostName
Items.Doc: The machine's name, or `null` when the system does not say.

Items.Name: userName
Items.Doc: The current user's name, or `null` when the system does not say.

Items.Name: homeDir
Items.Doc: The user's home directory, or `null` when the system does not say.

Items.Name: cpuCount
Items.Doc:
How many cores the machine has, for programs that split their work. The VM itself is
single-threaded.

Items.Name: nowMillis
Items.Doc:
Milliseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC.

A number rather than a date type: dates, time zones and calendars are their own module. The
number is the same on every platform.

Items.Name: nowNanos
Items.Doc:
Nanoseconds from a monotonic clock. Not comparable with `nowMillis`; the origin is arbitrary.
A system clock can jump during a measurement, a monotonic one cannot.

Items.Name: sleep
Items.Doc: Suspends the process. The VM is single-threaded, so nothing runs alongside.

Items.Name: envOr
Items.Signature: pub fn envOr(name: string, fallback: string): string
Items.Doc: An environment variable with a default.

Modules.Doc:
Child processes for tasks: `start` a program, `write` to its stdin, `readSomeOut`/
`readSomeErr` its streams, `wait` for its exit code — every waiting form yielding to the
scheduler instead of blocking the thread.

The silent forms answer *whether* (`null`/`false`); the `OrThrow` twins say *why* with an
`IoError` — `NotFound` when the program does not exist, `PermissionDenied` when it may not
be run. The streams speak `readSome`'s three truths: bytes are bytes, an EMPTY array is
the stream being done (EOF), and `null` is a failure.

Carries `processAccess`, its own capability bit: starting programs is a new power, not an
`osAccess` refinement.

Items.Name: Child
Items.Doc: A started child process. Opaque: it is issued here, never assembled.

Items.Name: start
Items.Signature: pub fn start(program: string, args: string[]): ?Child
Items.Doc:
Starts `program` with `args`, streams piped. `null` when it cannot start —
`startOrThrow` says why, `NotFound` being the usual answer.

Items.Name: startOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn startOrThrow(program: string, args: string[]): Child throws IoError
Items.Doc: `start`, with the reason when the program cannot start.

Items.Name: readSomeOut
Items.Signature: pub fn readSomeOut(child: Child, max: int): ?uint8[]
Items.Doc:
Waits for bytes on the child's standard output and reads up to `max` of them. Three
truths in one answer: bytes are bytes, an EMPTY array is the stream being done (EOF),
and `null` is a failure — `readSomeOutOrThrow` says which.

A `max` of zero or less PANICS: an empty answer already means EOF, so there is no
honest value to hand back for it.

Items.Name: readSomeOutOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn readSomeOutOrThrow(child: Child, max: int): uint8[] throws IoError
Items.Doc: `readSomeOut`, with the reason when the stream broke. EOF stays the empty array.

Items.Name: readSomeErr
Items.Signature: pub fn readSomeErr(child: Child, max: int): ?uint8[]
Items.Doc: `readSomeOut`, for the child's standard error.

Items.Name: readSomeErrOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn readSomeErrOrThrow(child: Child, max: int): uint8[] throws IoError
Items.Doc: `readSomeErr`, with the reason when the stream broke.

Items.Name: write
Items.Signature: pub fn write(child: Child, bytes: uint8[]): bool
Items.Doc:
Hands `bytes` to the child's standard input. The write is queued and drained in the
background; `false` once the child's stdin broke — a child that exited without reading
everything is the usual way.

Items.Name: writeOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn writeOrThrow(child: Child, bytes: uint8[]): void throws IoError
Items.Doc: `write`, with the reason when the child's stdin broke.

Items.Name: closeStdin
Items.Doc:
Closes the child's standard input once everything queued is written — EOF is how a
filter learns it has everything.

Items.Name: wait
Items.Doc: Waits until the child has exited and answers its exit code.

Items.Name: kill
Items.Doc:
Ends the child now, without appeal. The exit code `wait` then reports is the kill's,
not the program's.

Items.Name: close
Items.Doc:
Releases the child's resources — buffers, pipes, the notify descriptor. Closing twice
closes once; a running child is NOT stopped, only disowned.

Items.Name: secureRandom
Items.Doc:
`count` bytes from the operating system's cryptographic source — the ONE thing in this
module that is not deterministic, and deliberately so marked: keys, tokens and session ids
need entropy no seed can replay, which is exactly what makes it useless for a simulation
that wants to be reproduced. A negative `count` panics; zero answers the empty array.

Capability-free like the rest of the module: the source reaches no file, no clock and no
network — an embedded host loses nothing by a guest that can draw good dice.

Items.Name: Random
Items.Doc:
A deterministic pseudo-random generator (xorshift64*): one `int` of state, seeded by the
caller. Not cryptographic — keys need a source from the operating system, which is what
`secureRandom` is.

Members.Name: state
Members.Doc: The generator state; every draw replaces it.

Members.Name: seeded
Members.Signature: pub static fn seeded(seed: int): Random
Members.Doc:
A generator with an explicit seed. A seed of 0 is a fixed point for xorshift — the
sequence would stay 0 forever — so it is replaced silently rather than panicking on a
plausible input.

Members.Name: fresh
Members.Doc:
A generator seeded from the operating system's entropy — for a game or a shuffle that
should differ per run, and that nobody needs to replay. `seeded` is the reproducible
form; this one says in its name that the run cannot be repeated.

Members.Name: nextInt
Members.Doc: The next raw value. It may have either sign.

Members.Name: nextIntRange
Members.Signature: pub mut fn nextIntRange(lo: int, hi: int): int
Members.Doc: Uniformly distributed in `[lo, hi)`. An empty range yields `lo`.

Members.Name: nextFloat
Members.Doc: Uniformly distributed in `[0, 1)`.

Members.Name: nextBool
Members.Doc: True or false, from the next draw's parity.

Members.Name: nextGaussian
Members.Doc: Normally distributed, mean 0 and deviation 1 (Box–Muller).

Items.Name: shuffle
Items.Signature: pub fn shuffle<T>(random: Random, xs: List<T>): void
Items.Doc: Shuffles in place, Fisher–Yates: every permutation equally likely, one draw per element.

Items.Name: choice
Items.Signature: pub fn choice<T>(random: Random, xs: List<T>): ?T
Items.Doc: One element drawn uniformly, or `null` from an empty list.

Modules.Doc:
A failure as a value: `Ok(value)` or `Err(reason)`, and the combinators that compute with
either without testing first.

`throws` remains the language's mechanism; this is the holder for a failure that is stored,
collected or handled later. `orThrow` and `fromOptional` are the bridges to `throws` and `?T`.

Items.Name: Result
Items.Doc:
The outcome of something that can fail: the value, or the reason it did not happen.

Two variants and nothing else, so a `match` covers it with two arms. The reason type `E` is
unconstrained — a `string` is a fine reason for a config line, and `orThrow` alone asks for
a `Throwable`.

Members.Name: Ok
Members.Doc: It happened, and this is the value.

Members.Name: Err
Members.Doc: It did not, and this says why.

Members.Name: isOk
Members.Doc: Whether this is an `Ok`.

Members.Name: isErr
Members.Doc: Whether this is an `Err`.

Members.Name: ok
Members.Doc:
The value as an optional: `null` for an `Err`, which drops the reason — the bridge to
`??` and to every function that takes a `?T`.

Not available when `T` is itself optional: the answer would be `??T`. A `match` tells
`Ok(null)` from `Ok(v)` there, which is the distinction this would have collapsed anyway.

Members.Name: err
Members.Doc: The reason as an optional: `null` for an `Ok`.

Members.Name: unwrapOr
Members.Doc:
The value, or `fallback` for an `Err`. The fallback is evaluated either way; for one that
costs something, `unwrapOrElse` takes a function.

Members.Name: unwrapOrElse
Members.Signature: pub fn unwrapOrElse(fallback: fn(E) -> T): T
Members.Doc:
The value, or what `fallback` makes of the reason — the reason is not lost, it is handed
to the function that decides what stands in for the value.

Members.Name: expect
Members.Doc:
The value, or a panic carrying `message` — for a result that CANNOT be an `Err` here,
where being wrong about that is a programming error. As `std.option.expect` for `?T`.

Items.Name: map
Items.Signature: pub fn map<T, E, U>(r: Result<T, E>, f: fn(T) -> U): Result<U, E>
Items.Doc: Applies `f` to the value when there is one; an `Err` passes through unchanged.

Items.Name: mapErr
Items.Signature: pub fn mapErr<T, E, F>(r: Result<T, E>, f: fn(E) -> F): Result<T, F>
Items.Doc:
Applies `f` to the REASON when there is one; an `Ok` passes through unchanged. What a
layer uses to translate a lower layer's reason into its own.

Items.Name: andThen
Items.Signature: pub fn andThen<T, E, U>(r: Result<T, E>, f: fn(T) -> Result<U, E>): Result<U, E>
Items.Doc:
As `map`, but `f` may itself fail: the first `Err` in a chain wins, and everything after it
is skipped. `andThen(andThen(parse(a), lookup), validate)` reads as the three steps it is.

Items.Name: orElse
Items.Signature: pub fn orElse<T, E, F>(r: Result<T, E>, f: fn(E) -> Result<T, F>): Result<T, F>
Items.Doc:
A second attempt when the first failed: `f` gets the reason and answers a result of its own.
The mirror image of `andThen`.

Items.Name: orThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn orThrow<T, E :: [Throwable]>(r: Result<T, E>): T throws E
Items.Doc:
The value, or the reason THROWN — the bridge from the value form back to the language's
mechanism, for the moment a stored failure is finally handled.

The catch that goes with it is `catch (e: Throwable)` today: the compiler substitutes a
throws clause's type parameter at no call site yet, so a `catch (e: IoError)` beside it is
reported as not covering. That is a compiler limitation, not a property of this function.

Items.Name: fromOptional
Items.Signature: pub fn fromOptional<T, E>(o: ?T, error: E): Result<T, E>
Items.Doc:
An optional with a reason attached: the value when there is one, `error` when there is not.
What turns a `Map.get` or a `parseInt` into a result without a `match` at every site.

Not instantiable for an optional `T`, for the reason `ok` is not: the parameter would read
`??T`. `Result<?U, E>.Ok(value)` is the direct construction there.

Items.Name: concat
Items.Signature: pub fn concat(a: string, b: string): string
Items.Doc: The two joined — what `+` on strings compiles to.

Items.Name: fromInt
Items.Doc: The decimal text of the value.

Items.Name: fromUint
Items.Doc: The decimal text of an unsigned value.

Items.Name: fromFloat
Items.Doc: The decimal text of the value.

Items.Name: fromBool
Items.Doc: `"true"` or `"false"`.

Items.Name: fromChar
Items.Doc: The character as a one-character string.

Items.Name: repeat
Items.Signature: pub fn repeat(value: string, count: int): string
Items.Doc: The string repeated `count` times — what `s * n` compiles to.

Items.Name: fromChars
Items.Doc:
The characters joined back into one string — the inverse of `toChars`. Native since v1.14:
one call instead of one string per character.

Items.Name: utf8Decode
Items.Doc:
The bytes as a string, STRICTLY: invalid UTF-8 answers `null` rather than a U+FFFD quietly
standing in for the data — the difference to `std.io.file.text`, whose replacement decoding is
documented there.

Items.Name: Utf8Error
Items.Doc: Where a byte sequence stopped being UTF-8: the 0-based offset of the byte that broke it.

Items.Name: utf8DecodeOrThrow
Items.Signature: pub fn utf8DecodeOrThrow(bytes: uint8[]): string throws Utf8Error
Items.Doc: `utf8Decode`, with the reason when the bytes are not UTF-8: which byte broke the sequence.

Items.Name: isAlpha
Items.Doc: An ASCII letter.

Items.Name: isAlphanumeric
Items.Doc: An ASCII letter or a digit.

Items.Name: isWhitespace
Items.Doc:
Whether the character is white space in the Unicode sense — the same set `trim` removes,
so `s.trim() == s.trimStart().trimEnd()` and `isBlank` agree with it: the ASCII controls
`\t`..`\r` and the space, U+0085, U+00A0 and the other space separators (U+1680,
U+2000..U+200A, U+2028, U+2029, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000). Before 4.5 only four ASCII
characters counted here while `trim` already used this set.

Items.Name: isUpper
Items.Doc: `'A'` through `'Z'`.

Items.Name: isLower
Items.Doc: `'a'` through `'z'`.

Items.Name: charToDigit
Items.Doc:
The numeric value of a digit, or `null` when it is not one.

`?int` rather than `-1`: a failure the caller has to handle belongs in the type.

Items.Name: digitToChar
Items.Doc: The digit as a character, or `null` outside `0..9`.

Items.Name: join
Items.Signature: pub fn join(parts: string[], separator: string): string
Items.Doc:
Joins the parts with a separator: the inverse of `split`. One native call — a left fold
would copy the whole result once per part.

Items.Name: parseInt
Items.Doc:
`"-42"` becomes `-42`, anything else `null` — an empty text, a sign on its own, a character
that is no digit, and since 4.5 a magnitude beyond `int`, which used to wrap silently. The
reason is what `parseIntOrErr` says.

Items.Name: parseIntRadix
Items.Signature: pub fn parseIntRadix(value: string, radix: int): ?int
Items.Doc:
From a base of 2 to 36. Letters continue from `a`/`A`. `null` on anything `parseInt`
refuses, and on a base outside `2..=36`.

Items.Name: ParseErrorKind
Items.Doc: What kept a text from being a number.

Members.Name: Empty
Members.Doc: Nothing to read: the text is empty, or a sign with nothing after it.

Members.Name: InvalidDigit
Members.Doc: A character that is no digit of the base — `offset` says which.

Members.Name: Overflow
Members.Doc: The digits are fine and the number is not: it lies outside `int`.

Items.Name: ParseError
Items.Doc:
Why a text is not a number: which kind, and at which code-point offset the reading stopped.

The carrier-plus-kind shape of `std.io.error.IoError`: a class that throws, holding an enum
that matches, so a kind can be added without breaking a `match` over the ones known.

Members.Name: kind
Members.Doc: What went wrong.

Members.Name: offset
Members.Doc: Where the reading stopped, in code points; the text's length for `Overflow` and `Empty`.

Items.Name: parseIntOrErr
Items.Signature: pub fn parseIntOrErr(value: string): Result<int, ParseError>
Items.Doc:
`parseInt`, with the reason when the text is not a number: the value, or a `ParseError`
saying what stopped the reading and where.

Items.Name: parseIntRadixOrErr
Items.Signature: pub fn parseIntRadixOrErr(value: string, radix: int): Result<int, ParseError>
Items.Doc:
`parseIntRadix`, with the reason. A base outside `2..=36` is reported as `InvalidDigit` at
offset 0: no character of any text is a digit of a base that does not exist.

Items.Name: parseBool
Items.Doc: Exactly `"true"` or `"false"`; anything else is `null`.

Items.Name: parseFloat
Items.Doc:
The closest `float` to the decimal the text spells — `"3.5"`, `"-0.25"`, `".5"`, `"42"`,
exponent notation included (`"1e-6"`, `"2.5E3"`) — or `null` when the text spells none.
Strict about shape: no whitespace, no separators, and the words `NaN` and `Infinity` are not
numbers. A magnitude beyond the type rounds to the infinities, as IEEE 754 prescribes.

Native because the conversion is CORRECTLY ROUNDED, which needs arbitrary-precision
arithmetic in the worst cases; an approximate parser hands back a float the text did not
say. `parseFloat(fromFloat(x))` is `x` again, for every finite `x`.

Items.Name: StringBuilder
Items.Doc:
Builds a string piece by piece.

`s = s + part` in a loop is quadratic: every step copies the whole string so far. The builder
collects the parts and joins them once.

The backing is a doubling `string[]`, written by hand because this module must not import
`std.collections`.

Members.Name: parts
Members.Doc: The collected pieces; `count` says how many are filled.

Members.Name: count
Members.Doc: How many entries of `parts` are real.

Members.Name: new
Members.Doc: An empty builder.

Members.Name: append
Members.Signature: pub mut fn append(value: string): void
Members.Doc: Adds a piece; the backing array doubles when full.

Members.Name: appendLine
Members.Signature: pub mut fn appendLine(value: string): void
Members.Doc: Adds the piece and a `\n`.

Members.Name: appendChar
Members.Signature: pub mut fn appendChar(value: char): void
Members.Doc: Adds one character.

Members.Name: build
Members.Doc:
The pieces joined once — the point of collecting them. One native call over the filled
slice; a left fold would copy the whole result once per piece, the exact cost the
builder exists to avoid. Reads and never consumes: building twice yields the same
string.

Modules.Doc:
Cooperative tasks: `spawn` a `Coroutine<Wait>`, then `run()` drives every task to its end.

A task settles its own errors — `spawn` takes the non-throwing coroutine type, because the
scheduler has nobody to hand an exception to. A panic anywhere ends the program, as panics
do.

Items.Name: Wait
Items.Doc: What a yielded value asks the scheduler for.

Members.Name: Now
Members.Doc: Run me again once everyone before me had a turn — the cooperative "make room".

Members.Name: Sleep
Members.Doc:
Wake me after this many milliseconds. Sleepers wake in deadline order — two deadlines
that pass in the same poll still wake nearest-first, and a deadline already in the past
(a zero or negative wait) is due at the very next poll.

Members.Name: Readable
Members.Doc: Wake me when this descriptor has bytes to read. Descriptors come from `std.io.net`.

Members.Name: Writable
Members.Doc: Wake me when this descriptor can take bytes.

Members.Name: Interrupt
Members.Doc:
Wake me on an interrupt: Ctrl+C in a standalone program, or `interrupt()` from inside.
The clean-shutdown seat — a server parks a task here, and the wake is its signal to
close listeners and let `run` drain. Every parked task wakes on one interrupt.

Items.Name: interrupt
Items.Doc:
Wakes every task parked on `Wait.Interrupt`, exactly as Ctrl+C does — a server telling
itself to shut down: a task that decides "we are done" interrupts, the parked shutdown
task closes the listeners, and `run` drains. With nobody parked the interrupt is
REMEMBERED and taken by the next task to park — a signal, not a broadcast into the void.

Items.Name: spawn
Items.Doc:
Adds a task to the back of the run queue. Nothing runs before `run` does; spawning from
inside a running task is ordinary and the new task gets its turn in the same round.

Items.Name: pending
Items.Doc:
How many tasks the scheduler holds, whatever they are waiting for. Zero after `run`
returns; useful to a host deciding whether another `run` is worth calling.

Items.Name: run
Items.Doc:
Drives every task to its end and returns when none is left.

Ready tasks run round-robin, one step per turn. When none is ready, the scheduler blocks in
`poll` until the nearest deadline passes, a descriptor readies, or — with a task parked on
`Wait.Interrupt` — Ctrl+C arrives; the thread sleeps, it does not spin. A run holding ONLY
Interrupt tasks therefore waits, quietly and indefinitely, for the interrupt that is its
whole purpose.

Modules.Doc:
Marking tests, and the assertions that fail them. `lyric test` runs every function marked
`@Test` in the project's test root; a test fails by panicking, which is what the assertions
here do.

Items.Name: Test
Items.Doc:
Marks a top-level function as a test. `lyric test` finds it through the attribute row and
runs it in a fresh instance; the function takes no parameters and returns nothing.

Items.Name: assertTrue
Items.Signature: pub fn assertTrue(condition: bool, message: string): void
Items.Doc:
Fails the test with `message` when `condition` is false.

The same behavior as `std.core.assert` — it exists so a test file needs one import, and it
delegates so there is one implementation.

Items.Name: assertEq
Items.Signature: pub fn assertEq<T :: [Equatable<T>, Display]>(actual: T, expected: T): void
Items.Doc: Fails the test when the two values differ, naming both.

Items.Name: assertNotEq
Items.Signature: pub fn assertNotEq<T :: [Equatable<T>, Display]>(actual: T, unexpected: T): void
Items.Doc:
Fails the test when the two values are EQUAL, naming the value — the assertion for "it
changed", where `assertEq` says "it is".

Items.Name: assertNull
Items.Doc: Fails the test when the value is present, naming it.

Items.Name: assertNotNull
Items.Signature: pub fn assertNotNull<T>(value: ?T, message: string): void
Items.Doc: Fails the test when the value is absent.

Items.Name: assertClose
Items.Signature: pub fn assertClose(actual: float, expected: float, tolerance: float): void
Items.Doc:
Fails the test when the two floats lie further apart than `tolerance` — the comparison
`assertEq` cannot make for floating point, where `0.1 + 0.2` is not `0.3`. NaN on either
side fails: it is close to nothing.

Items.Name: assertLess
Items.Signature: pub fn assertLess<T :: [Ordered<T>, Display]>(actual: T, bound: T): void
Items.Doc: Fails the test when `actual` is not strictly less than `bound`, naming both.

Items.Name: assertContains
Items.Signature: pub fn assertContains(haystack: string, needle: string): void
Items.Doc: Fails the test when the text does not contain `needle`, quoting both.

Items.Name: fail
Items.Doc:
Fails the test outright, with `message` — for a branch a test must never reach.

`void` rather than `never` like `panic`: it does not count as a `return` for the flow
analysis until the language lets a library function say `never`.

Items.Name: Duration
Items.Signature: pub struct Duration :: [Equatable<Duration>, Ordered<Duration>, Hashable<Duration>, Display]
Items.Doc:
A distance between two instants, in whole milliseconds. May be negative: `a.since(b)` with
`b` later than `a` says so rather than hiding it.

Members.Name: millis
Members.Doc: The distance in milliseconds; the sign is the direction.

Members.Name: ofMillis
Members.Signature: pub static fn ofMillis(value: int): Duration
Members.Doc: A duration of whole milliseconds.

Members.Name: ofSeconds
Members.Signature: pub static fn ofSeconds(value: int): Duration
Members.Doc: A duration of whole seconds.

Members.Name: ofMinutes
Members.Signature: pub static fn ofMinutes(value: int): Duration
Members.Doc: A duration of whole minutes.

Members.Name: totalMillis
Members.Doc: The whole distance in milliseconds.

Members.Name: totalSeconds
Members.Doc: The whole distance in seconds, truncated towards zero.

Members.Name: plus
Members.Doc: The two added.

Members.Name: minus
Members.Doc: The other subtracted from this one.

Members.Name: equals
Members.Doc: Whether the two span the same distance.

Members.Name: compare
Members.Doc:
The shorter distance first; a negative duration comes before a positive one.

Three comparisons rather than `this.millis - other.millis`: that subtraction overflows
for two durations far enough apart and hands back the opposite sign.

Members.Name: hash
Members.Doc: The millisecond count, which is what `int` hashes to.

Members.Name: show
Members.Doc:
The distance with its unit: `1500ms`, `-500ms`.

Milliseconds, not a scaled `1.5s`: this type counts whole milliseconds, and a rendering
that divides them invents a precision the value does not carry. Scaled forms are
`std.fmt` work.

Items.Name: TimeError
Items.Doc: A failed reading of a time text: what was handed in, and what broke.

Members.Name: text
Members.Doc: What went wrong, naming the field that broke.

Items.Name: Instant
Items.Signature: pub struct Instant :: [Equatable<Instant>, Ordered<Instant>, Hashable<Instant>, Display]
Items.Doc: A point on the wall clock: milliseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC.

Members.Name: millis
Members.Doc: Milliseconds since the epoch; negative is before 1970.

Members.Name: now
Members.Doc: The wall clock, now.

Members.Name: ofEpochMillis
Members.Signature: pub static fn ofEpochMillis(value: int): Instant
Members.Doc:
The instant at these epoch milliseconds — for stored timestamps and for tests, which
want a clock that stands still.

Members.Name: epochMillis
Members.Doc: Milliseconds since the epoch — the raw number back, for storing.

Members.Name: since
Members.Doc: The distance from `earlier` to this instant. Negative when `earlier` is actually later.

Members.Name: plus
Members.Doc: This instant moved by a duration; a negative one moves backwards.

Members.Name: iso
Members.Doc:
ISO 8601 in UTC, millisecond precision: `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`.

`divFloor`/`modFloor` rather than `/` and `%`, so an instant BEFORE the epoch lands in
the right day — truncation would round the day towards 1970 and hand the rest a negative
time.

Members.Name: fromIso
Members.Doc:
Reads what `iso()` writes — the round-trip half that was missing since `iso` exists:
`fromIso(x.iso())` is `x`, pre-epoch instants included. `null` when the text is not
that shape or names a day that does not exist; `fromIsoOrThrow` says which field broke.

Strict on purpose: exactly `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.mmmZ`, UTC only. A parser that accepts
offsets or shortened forms would be promising calendar arithmetic this module does not
have; the day `31` of February is refused rather than silently carried into March.

Members.Name: fromIsoOrThrow
Members.Signature: pub static fn fromIsoOrThrow(text: string): Instant throws TimeError
Members.Doc: `fromIso`, with the reason when the text does not read.

Members.Name: equals
Members.Doc: Whether the two name the same point on the clock.

Members.Name: compare
Members.Doc:
The earlier instant first.

Three comparisons rather than `this.millis - other.millis`: an instant near the epoch
against one near the type's maximum overflows that subtraction, and the sign it hands
back is the wrong one.

Members.Name: hash
Members.Doc: The epoch milliseconds, which is what `int` hashes to.

Members.Name: show
Members.Doc:
The ISO 8601 form — the same text `iso()` writes, because it is the one textual shape
this type has.
